channel.title: The Fuel Guys Blog
channel.description: Straight answers about mobile diesel delivery in Denver: dyed vs. clear diesel rules, DEF, generator refueling, costs, and emergency fuel service.

item.title: How Much Diesel Should You Keep on a Job Site?
item.description: Size the tank to your burn, not to the biggest one the rental yard has. Multiply your daily fuel use by the days between deliveries and add one day of reserve. Then check that number against four thresholds - 60 gallons, 660, 1,100 and 1,320 - because each one adds a rule.

item.title: What Does "24/7 Emergency Fuel Delivery" Actually Mean?
item.description: "24/7 emergency fuel delivery" is a marketing phrase, not a regulated term - no agency defines or enforces it. What decides whether fuel reaches you at 2 a.m. is who answers the phone, whether a loaded truck is staged, and whether a driver still has legal hours under federal hours-of-service rules.

item.title: Does Your Building's Generator Fuel Meet Its Load-Test Requirement?
item.description: No - passing a load test does not prove your fuel. NFPA 110 treats them as separate obligations: section 8.4.2 requires a monthly 30-minute run at 30 percent of nameplate kW, while section 8.3.7 requires a separate annual fuel quality test to ASTM standards. Required testing burns so little diesel that a Class 48 tank can sit for years.

item.title: What Happens If a Backup Generator Runs Out of Fuel Mid-Outage?
item.description: The engine stops and the building goes dark until utility power comes back. Running a tank to the bottom pulls air into the injection system, so the generator will not restart the moment fuel arrives - the fuel system has to be bled and primed first. Plan on hours, not minutes.

item.title: How Long Will a Generator Run on a Full Tank?
item.description: Runtime equals usable tank gallons divided by fuel burn at your actual load, not at nameplate. A 100 kW Generac SD100 burns 7.3 gal/hr at full load and 4.2 gal/hr at half, so its 90-gallon tank runs about 12 hours loaded or 21 hours at half. Load moves runtime further than tank size does.

item.title: Why Does DEF Go Bad in Summer Heat?
item.description: Heat breaks urea down into ammonia, and DEF's 32.5% urea concentration drifts below the ISO 22241 minimum. Shelf life is set by storage temperature, not the calendar: 12 months at 86F, 6 months at 95F, and above 95F every batch should be tested before use.

item.title: How Do You Stop Diesel Theft on a Denver Job Site?
item.description: You stop job-site diesel theft by removing the target and controlling the paperwork. Lock and fence the tank, meter every gallon in and out, reconcile fuel against machine hours weekly, and keep less fuel on site by scheduling deliveries closer to burn. Cameras help only if someone is assigned to review the footage.

item.title: What Is Wet Hosing, and Is It Cheaper Than a Job-Site Tank?
item.description: Wet hosing is direct-to-equipment fueling: a fuel truck comes to your site and fills each machine from the hose, usually overnight. It is cheaper than a job-site tank when your burn is modest or the job is short, because you pay for fuel and delivery only: no tank, no fire permit, no spill plan, no crew time spent fueling.

item.title: How Much Diesel Does an Excavator Burn Per Hour?
item.description: A 20-tonne excavator like a Cat 320 burns 2.4 to 3.7 gallons of diesel per hour. A 13-tonne machine burns 1.6 to 2.6 gallons; a 36-tonne machine burns 4.9 to 7.8. Caterpillar's low figures assume 50 percent idle time and the high figures 10 percent, so idling drives most of the spread.

item.title: Do You Need a Permit to Store Diesel on a Denver Job Site?
item.description: Usually, yes. Most Denver-metro fire departments require an operational permit once a temporary outdoor diesel tank exceeds 60 gallons. OSHA adds its own rules on top: containers 20 feet from buildings, 1,100 gallons maximum per group, and an extinguisher within 75 feet. Thresholds vary by jurisdiction - confirm with your local fire authority.

item.title: How Much Does Mobile Diesel Delivery Cost in Denver?
item.description: Most Denver mobile diesel deliveries are priced as the day's market rate per gallon plus a delivery fee. Recent delivered ranges: $3.69-$4.69/gal for on-road diesel and $3.09-$4.09/gal for off-road (dyed) diesel, with delivery fees from $0 to around $1,000 depending on volume, distance, and site difficulty. Emergency calls roughly double the delivery fee.
